title: "cleanplots Stata help file"

```{=html}
<div class="stata-help">
<pre>
<span class="result"><u>Title</u></span>
<br/>
    <span class="result">cleanplots</span> --
               Graphics scheme that implements best data visualization
               practices. Colors are color-blind friendly and remain
               distinguishable when printed in black and white, with
               coordinated marker symbols and line patterns so that groups stay
               distinct across multiple visual channels.
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>Overview</u></span>
<br/>
    <span class="result">cleanplots</span> changes the default look and feel of Stata graphics.  The
    choices of colors, markers, line patterns, gridlines, legend placement,
    and other aspects of the figure follow best data visualization practices,
    with no per-graph effort needed.
<br/>
    The color palette is designed for accessibility. It contains no red-green
    pair (red-green color blindness is the most common form, affecting roughly
    8% of men), and the first five colors pass simulation checks for all three
    major forms of color blindness. The palette also alternates darker and
    lighter colors so that the first several groups remain distinguishable by
    lightness alone when a figure is printed in black and white.
<br/>
    Color alone reliably distinguishes about 4-5 groups. Beyond that,
    addiitonal markers or patterns are needed for distinguishability.
    <span class="result">cleanplots</span> automatically varies markers, line patterns, and other
    features.
<br/>
    Bar charts, area plots, and pie charts automatically use softer versions
    of the colors. These elements use far more ink than points and lines, so
    full-strength colors overwhelm; <span class="result">cleanplots</span> fades them for a cleaner look
    while full-strength colors remain on markers, lines, and outlines.
<br/>
    The default <span class="result">cleanplots</span> colors are a nominal palette, meaning no ordering
    is implied by the colors or markers. When an ordered (ordinal) palette is
    needed, use the <span class="result">cleanplots#</span> schemes on a single graph (see Ordinal color
    schemes below).
<br/>
    For more information and to see examples, see the cleanplots website here.
<br/>
    Many of the features of cleanplots are adapted from the excellent black
    and white colorscheme plotplain.
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>Using cleanplots</u></span>
<br/>
    To change your graphics scheme to <span class="result">cleanplots</span> for all graphs:
<br/>
        set scheme cleanplots, perm
<br/>
    Or apply it to a single graph with the <span class="result">scheme()</span> option:
<br/>
        sysuse auto, clear
        graph twoway scatter price weight, scheme(cleanplots)
<br/>
    Stata's default graphic scheme is <span class="result">s2color</span>. To change back to the default:
<br/>
        set scheme s2color, perm
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>The colors</u></span>
<br/>
    The ten main colors, used for markers, lines, and confidence intervals
    (shown as the Stata color definition and the resulting hex code):
<br/>
       <span class="result">#</span>               <span class="result">Definition</span>        <span class="result">Hex</span>        <span class="result">RGB</span>
       1               red*1.2          #D50000    213 0 0
       2               eltblue*.9       #8FC6EB    143 198 235
       3               black            #000000    0 0 0
       4               gs9              #909090    144 144 144
       5               purple*1.1       #740074    116 0 116
       6               pink*.3          #FFB3D9    255 179 217
       7               navy*1.3         #143755    20 55 85
       8               gs12             #C0C0C0    192 192 192
       9               gs4              #404040    64 64 64
       10              lavender*.35     #D9D7F0    217 215 240
<br/>
    Bars, areas, and pies use softer versions of the same colors (e.g.,
    eltblue*.7, purple*.9), rendered with 70% intensity. You can verify any of
    the colors interactively at Coloring for Colorblindness.
<br/>
<a name="ordinal"></a><span class="result"><u>Ordinal color schemes</u></span>
<br/>
    The default <span class="result">cleanplots</span> colors are nominal, with no implied ordering:
<br/>
        sysuse auto, clear
        graph bar price, over(rep78) asyvars scheme(cleanplots)
<br/>
    To have the colors reflect ordering, use the <span class="result">cleanplots#</span> schemes on a
    single graph. Five are available -- <span class="result">cleanplots3</span>, <span class="result">cleanplots5</span>, <span class="result">cleanplots7</span>,
    <span class="result">cleanplots9</span>, and <span class="result">cleanplots11</span> -- where the number is how many sequential
    colors the scheme provides. Colors run from light yellow to dark navy, so
    higher categories are darker. For example, for a chart with 5 ordered
    groups:
<br/>
        sysuse auto, clear
        graph bar price, over(rep78) asyvars scheme(cleanplots5)
<br/>
    The ordinal colors are from the cividis palette (Nunez, Anderton, &amp;
    Renslow 2018), a variant of viridis (van der Walt &amp; Smith 2015) optimized
    so that readers with red-green color blindness see essentially the same
    palette as everyone else. Because the colors run monotonically from light
    to dark, the ordering itself also survives black and white printing.
<br/>
    The <span class="result">cleanplots#</span> schemes inherit all layout, sizing, and legend settings
    from the main <span class="result">cleanplots</span> scheme, and each series gets a distinct line
    pattern and marker symbol for maximum distinguishability. If a graph has
    more groups than the scheme has colors, the colors recycle (e.g., under
    <span class="result">cleanplots3</span> the 4th group repeats color 1) while the line patterns and
    marker symbols continue to vary, so recycled groups never share both color
    and pattern/symbol.
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>Updates</u></span>
<br/>
    <span class="result">cleanplots</span> was overhauled in July 2026 to ensure all 10 colors and the
    choices of lines, markers, etc. are color-blind friendly and work as well
    as possible in black and white. In addiiton, the ordinal <span class="result">cleanplots#</span>
    schemes were added. Finally, the legend was moved to be at the direct
    right of the graph
<br/>
    I recommend using the updated scheme. But if you are feeling nostalgic,
    the older version is preserved as <span class="result">cleanplots_classic</span>.
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>cleanplots for R</u></span>
<br/>
    A companion <span class="result">cleanplots</span> package for R (ggplot2) shares this scheme's
    colors, marker symbols, line patterns, and layout. See the full
    documentation and details on downloading the R package at
    tdmize.github.io/cleanplots.
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>Authorship</u></span>
<br/>
    <span class="result">cleanplots</span> is written by Trenton D Mize (Departments of Sociology &amp;
    Statistics [by courtesy] &amp; The Methodology Center at Purdue University).
    Questions can be sent to tmize@purdue.edu
<br/>
<span class="result"><u>Citation &amp; References</u></span>
<br/>
    In general, I do not think the use of a graphics scheme requires citation.
    So for most cases, feel free to use cleanplots without citation.  But, if
    you need/want a citation you can cite cleanplots as:
<br/>
    Mize, Trenton D. 2017. "cleanplots: Stata graphics scheme for easy and
    effective data visualizations."
    https://www.trentonmize.com/software/cleanplots
<br/>
    If using the ordinal <span class="result">cleanplots#</span> schemes, please also credit the cividis
    colors:
<br/>
    Nunez, Jamie R., Christopher R. Anderton, and Ryan S. Renslow. 2018.
    "Optimizing colormaps with consideration for color vision deficiency to
    enable accurate interpretation of scientific data." PLOS ONE 13(7):
    e0199239.
</pre>
</div>
```
